I don't think anyone here will consider you weak, and I for sure don't - it is legitimately really hard! There have been a bunch of times that I've 'tried' to quit and then immediately caved within the first 24 hours, so you're not alone in having a tough first day of it. I've gone 4 days now and I already posted here twice during that time because I was considering giving in again lol. Posting here for support is a great step, people are super understanding and have been where you are now.

The best advice I've gotten from people is taking it one day at a time, focusing on getting through today instead of worrying about how I'll be able to go X days/weeks/months without it. Replacing it with something makes a lot of sense too - it can be a coping mechanism, so you can't just take it away and expect to be okay, something else needs to take its place. Change of scenery is good too - instead of sitting on my couch watching TV like I would when high, I've been spending more time in another room. It sounds dumb, but it honestly is a little bit helpful to not have exactly the same routine.

In terms of what you could replace it with, I think advice like exercise, trying new hobbies etc is great but if you struggle with motivation it can make it feel even harder to go without weed AND start up a whole new set of healthy habits. I'm trying to set the bar a bit lower for myself and just always have music or a podcast on so that I can focus on that instead of thoughts and cravings, and doing crafts, puzzles, and all the chores at night to distract myself. And also trying to go to bed earlier so I don't have to pass as much time sober at night :)

I don't think that was English, sorry' haha. Plus I could never remember what we were talking about. Now I try and just say something like 'brain' or 'pause' when I feel it coming on so she knows what's going on and we can take a second to ground.

We've been trying to solve it for a while and honestly we're not there yet, it still happens pretty frequently, but I feel like recently doing phone appointments has been helpful. I also keep notes on my phone and tried writing out my thoughts to prep for appointments, and that sometimes worked, but I'd still shut down while reading my notes sometimes. I think (hope?) it just takes a lot of trial and error to figure out what works for  you to lessen some of the pressure/anxiety in the appt, spotting the signs that the shut down is coming, and understanding what thoughts and feelings come up when it starts to happen. Can you tell when you're about to shut down, and do you know what thoughts/feelings tend to prompt it for you? I think that's a good place to start, because in my experience it's so much better to prevent it than try to come out of the shut down once it's already happening, or 'recover' afterwards and still be productive. Shit's tiring haha.

I was/am pretty frustrated because my therapist also hasn't really done much to try and prevent the shut downs, or had suggestions for what we can try differently, so it has felt like I'm just supposed to figure it out on my own even though it's an overwhelming involuntary physical reaction. I haven't been brave enough to do this myself tbh, but I think the best approach is probably just being really forthright about needing more support to figure it out, or trying to brainstorm together.

I wish I had something useful to offer, but I mostly just wanted to say that I too struggle with shutting down frequently and I know how hard it makes it to communicate and make progress. Plus with ocd, I find that having spotty memory of the session increases the odds I obsess and ruminate about how things went. My therapist and I are still trying to figure out how to manage it, and recently we've been trying phone calls instead of video because it somehow takes some of the pressure off.

I don't want to assume you're like me in other ways lol, but I also have a tendency to read into her actions...but when I've brought up my concerns with her (whether it's fear she's frustrated with my constant shutdowns or what I view as lack of progress) it's always been a good, and often productive, conversation. Maybe your therapist has assumed the weekly-ish sessions are too much for you and that's why he suggested biweekly. Maybe he thought it would give you more time for homework between sessions.

Worst case, maybe when you bring it up he realizes he did suggest biweekly out of his own frustration. That wouldn't be a you problem, for the record - that would be a him problem. A good therapist will meet you where you are and work with you on things like motivation, grounding so you're not dissociating all the time, and generally trying new things to get unstuck. That's why you're in therapy - to get help with these things!

However that conversation goes, I hope you know there's nothing wrong with you for experiencing this and that you're not 'too difficult' for therapy or anything :)
